findings.finding: 1 Maccabees 6:8 does not say the king was near the end of his life or on his deathbed; it says only that he fell upon his bed and became ill from sorrow. 'Greek king' is not in either text.
findings.before: Both passages say that a Greek king 'fell upon his bed' near the end of his life: Alexander knowing he was dying, Antiochus falling ill from sorrow at his failures. The repeated phrase links the two royal deathbeds in the same book.
findings.after: Both passages say that a ruler 'fell upon his bed': in 1:5 Alexander, knowing he was dying, and in 6:8 the king who 'became ill from sorrow, because things had not happened to him as he had intended.' The repeated phrase links the two royal collapses in the same book.

findings.finding: Neither shown text says 2:14 is mourning over the desecration of Jerusalem, or that 2:39 is over 'the slain'; those occasions are supplied from outside the passages.
findings.before: Both passages show Mattathias responding to disaster in the same way: he 'mourned greatly' over the desecration of Jerusalem in 2:14, and he and his friends 'mourned for them greatly' over the slain in 2:39. In 2:14 he is with his sons and adds torn garments and sackcloth.
findings.after: Both passages show Mattathias responding to disaster in the same way: in 2:14 he and his sons tore their garments, put on sackcloth and 'mourned greatly', and in 2:39 he and his friends 'mourned for them greatly'.

findings.finding: 'On the approach to Jerusalem' is not stated in either text; 7:39 says only that Nicanor went out from Jerusalem and encamped at Beth-horon.
findings.before: Beth-horon, where Judas meets Seron at the ascent, is also where Nicanor encamps and a force meets him. Both name the same place on the approach to Jerusalem, in the same spelling.
findings.after: Beth-horon, at whose ascent Judas went out with a few men to meet the enemy, is also where Nicanor, going out from Jerusalem, encamped and a Syrian force met him. Both name the same place in the same spelling.

findings.finding: Ammon is not named in 5:7; the campaign's target is supplied from outside the shown text.
findings.before: Judas's campaign against Ammon and Simon's in Galilee are told in nearly the same words: 'engaged them in many battles. They were crushed before him' and 'engaged the nations in many battles. The nations were crushed before him.' They are two parallel campaigns by two brothers.
findings.after: The campaign told in 5:7 and Simon's campaign in Galilee in 5:21 are told in nearly the same words: 'engaged them in many battles. They were crushed before him' and 'engaged the nations in many battles. The nations were crushed before him.' They are two parallel campaigns of the Maccabean brothers.

findings.finding: 1 Maccabees 5:37 does not call the army large or mention Judas, 2 Maccabees 12:20 does not say Timothy gathered an army, and neither text mentions a campaign 'beyond the Jordan'.
findings.before: Both passages describe Timothy gathering a large army against Judas (Maccabeus) during the campaign beyond the Jordan. 2 Maccabees gives his strength as one hundred twenty thousand infantry and twenty-five hundred horsemen but does not name Raphon or the stream.
findings.after: Both passages concern the army Timothy brought against the Jews in the same campaign: 1 Maccabees 5:37 says Timothy gathered another army and encamped opposite Raphon beyond the stream, and 2 Maccabees 12:20 has Maccabeus rush against Timothy, who had one hundred twenty thousand infantry and twenty-five hundred horsemen. 2 Maccabees does not name Raphon or the stream.

findings.finding: Neither text places Beth-shan 'on the route between the Jordan crossing and the plain'; 5:52 says only that the plain lay opposite Beth-shan.
findings.before: Tryphon later sets out and comes to Beth-shan, the same place named here in the same spelling, on the route between the Jordan crossing and the plain.
findings.after: In 1 Maccabees 12:40 Tryphon, seeking to seize Jonathan, sets out and comes to Beth-shan, the same place named here in the same spelling, opposite which the company crossed the Jordan into the great plain.

findings.finding: In 4:61 the force is stationed 'there' while Beth-zur is fortified; the rationale presents Beth-zur as the place 'where he stationed a force there to guard it', which the shown text does not clearly say.
findings.before: Beth-zur is the same fortress that Judas earlier fortified, where 'he stationed a force there to guard it'; here the king seizes it and 'stationed a garrison there to guard it'. The wording of the two garrison notices closely matches, though the occupying side is reversed.
findings.after: Beth-zur, which the king seizes and garrisons here, is the place fortified earlier in 4:61 'so that the people would have a stronghold facing Idumea.' The garrison wording is similar ('stationed a force there to guard it' / 'stationed a garrison there to guard it'), but the stronghold built for the people is now held by the king.

findings.finding: In 2 Maccabees 14:26 Alcimus denounces Nicanor's intentions to Demetrius; he does not denounce Judas, though he calls him 'the kingdom's conspirator'.
findings.before: Alcimus is the same man in both texts, acting against Judas: here Judas sees the evil Alcimus committed, and in the other account Alcimus goes to Demetrius and denounces Judas as 'the kingdom's conspirator'.
findings.after: Alcimus is the same man in both texts, set against Judas: here Judas sees the evil Alcimus and those with him committed among the sons of Israel, and in 2 Maccabees 14:26 Alcimus goes to Demetrius, says Nicanor's intentions were disloyal, and calls Judas 'the kingdom's conspirator'.

findings.finding: Neither shown text says Nicanor's encampment preceded a 'decisive battle with Judas'.
findings.before: Beth-horon is the same site in both texts: earlier Judas went out to meet Seron at 'the ascent of Beth-horon', and here Nicanor encamps at Beth-horon before his decisive battle with Judas.
findings.after: Beth-horon is the same site in both texts: in 3:16 Judas went out to meet the enemy at 'the ascent of Beth-horon', and here Nicanor goes out from Jerusalem and encamps at Beth-horon, where a Syrian force meets him.

findings.finding: The only link is the ordinary words 'wish' and 'exalted' applied to two unrelated powers (Rome and the ram of Daniel's vision); the rationale itself concedes it is wording only. Not a specific connection.
1 Maccabees 7:50 as shown does not mention Nicanor's death.
findings.before: Both close an episode after the death of an opponent with the same formula, 'The land of Judah was quiet', after Nicanor's death 'for a few days' and here after Alcimus's death 'for two years'.
findings.after: Both close an episode with the same formula, 'The land of Judah was quiet': in 7:50 'for a few days', and here, after Alcimus has died and Bacchides has returned to the king, 'for two years'.

findings.finding: The source does not contain 'all the festivals of Israel'; that phrase is only in Ezekiel 45:17. The source has 'appointed days'.
findings.before: Both list the sacred calendar as festivals, new moons and Sabbaths, together with all the festivals of Israel. The source adds the three days before and after each festival and makes them days of exemption, which the other text does not.
findings.after: Both list the sacred calendar as festivals, new moons and Sabbaths. Ezekiel adds 'all the festivals of the house of Israel' and makes these the occasions of the ruler's offerings; the source adds appointed days and the three days before and after each festival and makes them days of exemption and release.

findings.finding: The quoted phrase 'sabbaths, new moons, and feasts' is not in the source, which reads 'festivals, sabbaths, new moons, and appointed days'; the source also does not speak of 'the Lord's service'.
findings.before: Both name 'sabbaths, new moons, and feasts' as the appointed days of the Lord's service. The other text concerns burnt offerings on those days, not exemption from royal exactions.
findings.after: Both name the same sacred days: 1 Chronicles 23:31 has 'sabbaths, new moons, and feasts', and the source 'festivals, sabbaths, new moons, and appointed days'. The other text concerns burnt offerings on those days, not exemption from royal exactions.

findings.finding: In 10:63 'concerning any matter' goes with 'petition against him', while 'trouble' goes with 'concerning any charge'; the rationale splices the two phrases.
findings.before: Both are royal guarantees that no one may 'trouble' the protected party 'concerning any matter'. Here Demetrius offers this to all the Jews, while in the other text Alexander proclaims it for Jonathan personally.
findings.after: Both are royal guarantees of protection in similar words: here no one may exact payment from or 'trouble any of them concerning any matter', and in 10:63 it is proclaimed that 'no one may petition against him concerning any matter, and that no one may trouble him concerning any charge.' Here the guarantee covers all the Jews; in 10:63 it is for Jonathan personally.

findings.finding: 1 Maccabees 11:23 does not say Jonathan went to the king; it says he ordered the siege to continue, selected elders and priests, and exposed himself to danger.
findings.before: Jonathan 'exposed himself to danger' when he went to the king; the public decree later honours Simon and his brothers because they 'exposed themselves to danger' for the nation, using the same phrase for the same family.
findings.after: Jonathan 'exposed himself to danger' in 11:23; the public decree in 14:29 honours Simon son of Mattathias and his brothers because they 'exposed themselves to danger' for the nation, using the same phrase for the same family.

findings.finding: Ai is not named in the shown text of Joshua 8:19.
findings.before: The men in ambush 'rose from their positions' against Jonathan, echoing Joshua's ambush that 'rose quickly from its place' at Ai. Here the ambush is set against Israel's leader, whereas at Ai it was Israel's own.
findings.after: The men in ambush 'rose from their positions' and joined battle, echoing Joshua 8:19, where 'the ambush rose quickly from its place', captured the city and burned it. Here the ambush is set against Jonathan's army, whereas in Joshua it was Israel's own.

findings.finding: In Genesis 45:27 Jacob's spirit is rekindled when he saw the wagons Joseph had sent, after being told Joseph's words; not simply on hearing the words.
findings.before: When they heard the words, 'the spirit of the people was rekindled', just as 'the spirit of Jacob their father was rekindled' when he heard Joseph's words. The same distinctive phrase describes renewed spirit on hearing a message.
findings.after: When they heard these words, 'the spirit of the people was rekindled', just as 'the spirit of Jacob their father was rekindled' when he was told Joseph's words and saw the wagons Joseph had sent. The same distinctive phrase describes renewed spirit at good news.

findings.finding: Neither shown text mentions a Roman letter.
findings.before: Both verses state that Antiochus 'encamped against Dora'; the later verse resumes the siege narrative after the Roman letter. It does not repeat the figures of a hundred and twenty thousand warriors and eight thousand cavalry.
findings.after: Both verses state that Antiochus 'encamped against Dora'; the later verse resumes the siege, with Antiochus making siege engines and blocking Tryphon from going out or coming in. It does not repeat the figures of a hundred and twenty thousand warriors and eight thousand cavalry.

findings.finding: Nehemiah 9:32 is not the opening of its prayer; it begins 'Now, our God' partway through.
findings.before: Both prayers open by addressing God with the titles 'strong' and 'fearsome'. Nehemiah 9:32 calls Him 'mighty, great, strong and fearsome', and the source 'fearsome, strong, righteous and merciful'.
findings.after: Both prayers address God with the titles 'strong' and 'fearsome': Nehemiah 9:32 calls Him 'the mighty, great, strong and fearsome One', and the source 'fearsome, strong, righteous and merciful'.

findings.finding: The source as shown does not say the prayer was made on behalf of the people.
findings.before: Daniel's prayer addresses the 'Lord God' as 'great, strong, and fearsome', the same cluster of titles used here ('Lord God ... fearsome, strong'). Both are prayers made on behalf of the people.
findings.after: Daniel prays to the 'Lord God' and addresses Him as 'the great, strong, and fearsome God'; the prayer here likewise addresses the 'Lord God' as 'fearsome, strong'.

findings.finding: The source does not say the Greeks were mourning Onias; it says they shared the Jews' hatred of the wickedness. The closing sentence about other passages is unsupported.
findings.before: The Onias whose killing is protested is the high priest Onias introduced at 2 Maccabees 3:1, praised there for his piety and "hatred of wickedness"; the Greeks here share "their hatred of the wickedness" in mourning him. No other passage identifies the petition itself.
findings.after: The Onias whose senseless killing the Jews protest to the king is the high priest Onias introduced in 2 Maccabees 3:1, praised there for his piety and 'hatred of wickedness'.

findings.finding: Neither text says Lysimachus's actions as deputy were the matters behind the trial.
findings.before: The Menelaus brought to trial is the Menelaus who left his own brother Lysimachus as his deputy in the high priesthood; Lysimachus's actions as that deputy are the matters behind the trial.
findings.after: The Menelaus brought to trial here is the Menelaus of 2 Maccabees 4:29, who left his own brother Lysimachus as his deputy in the high priesthood.

findings.finding: Daniel 8:23 does not speak of divine judgment, only of a king arising when sins reach fullness; and 2 Maccabees 6:15 as shown does not say God disciplines Israel early.
findings.before: Both tie divine judgment to the point when sins reach their limit: 2 Maccabees speaks of reaching "the end of our sins," and Daniel of the time "when their sins reach fullness." 2 Maccabees uses the idea to explain why God disciplines Israel early rather than waiting.
findings.after: Both mark a time when sins reach their limit: 2 Maccabees speaks of God not taking vengeance on us 'when we have reached the end of our sins', and Daniel of the end of their kingship, 'when their sins reach fullness', when a king with a shameless face will arise.

findings.finding: Neither shown text says the victims are Jews refusing to break faith.
findings.before: In both, a furious king orders the instrument of execution heated against Jews who refuse to break faith: Antiochus orders pans and cauldrons heated, and Nebuchadnezzar orders the furnace heated seven times.
findings.after: In both, a furious king orders an instrument of punishment heated: here the king becomes furious and orders pans and cauldrons heated, and Nebuchadnezzar, filled with fury, orders the furnace heated seven times beyond what was needed.

findings.finding: Neither shown text mentions seven men or the resurrection; the source says only 'after her sons', and Matthew 22:27 as shown is just 'Last of all, the woman died.'
findings.before: Both close an account of seven men with "Last of all" the woman dying. In Matthew the woman is the wife of seven brothers in a question about the resurrection, not this mother, but the story shape and the resurrection theme are shared.
findings.after: Both close a series of deaths with the same words, 'Last of all', and the death of the woman: here 'Last of all, after her sons, the mother died', and in Matthew 22:27 'Last of all, the woman died.'

findings.finding: The shown texts do not mention brothers, seven sons, or a dispute about the resurrection; Mark 12:22 says only 'The seven left no offspring'.
findings.before: Mark's version likewise ends the story of seven brothers with "Last of all, the woman also died," in a dispute about the resurrection, matching the close of this account of seven sons and their mother.
findings.after: Both close a series of deaths with the same words, 'Last of all', and the death of the woman: Mark 12:22 'The seven left no offspring. Last of all, the woman also died', and here 'Last of all, after her sons, the mother died.'

findings.finding: In 1 Maccabees 5:17 Judas does not give command to Jonathan; Jonathan goes with Judas to Gilead while Simon is told to choose men for Galilee.
findings.before: Simon and Jonathan are Judas's brothers in both passages, and in both Judas divides his forces and gives command to his brothers. Joseph, named only here, is not identified.
findings.after: Simon and Jonathan are Judas's brothers in both passages, and in both the forces are divided among the brothers: here Simon, Joseph and Jonathan each lead a division of fifteen hundred, and in 1 Maccabees 5:17 Simon takes men to Galilee while Judas and Jonathan go to Gilead. Joseph is named only here.

findings.finding: 'For his own advancement' is not in 2 Maccabees 14:4.
findings.before: Both texts describe a golden crown and a palm presented to a king Demetrius as a diplomatic gift. Here Alcimus brings them for his own advancement, whereas in the other text they were sent by Simon and acknowledged in a royal letter.
findings.after: Both texts describe a golden crown and a palm presented to King Demetrius as a diplomatic gift: here Alcimus brings them, together with temple branches, in the one hundred fifty-first year; in 1 Maccabees 13:37 a royal letter acknowledges 'the golden crown and the palm branch that you sent'.

findings.finding: No shared wording, event or image beyond the general theme of Moab's leaders being destroyed (Moab is not even named in the Amos verse shown); the label itself is 'shared theme'. Too vague for a link.
Amos 4:1 does not describe its addressees as complacent, and 6:1 speaks of those who trust in Samaria's mountain, not those on it.
findings.before: Both oracles in Amos are addressed to the complacent on 'Samaria's mountain': here those who trust in it, there the 'heifers of Bashan on Samaria's mountain' who oppress the poor.
findings.after: Both oracles in Amos name 'Samaria's mountain': here woe is pronounced on those who trust in it, and in 4:1 on the 'heifers of Bashan on Samaria's mountain' who oppress the poor.

findings.finding: In Amos 6:2 'their borders' refers to 'these kingdoms' generally, not specifically to Emath's borders.
findings.before: Both texts name Emath together with its borders: Amos asks whether Emath's 'borders are greater than your borders', and Zechariah's oracle mentions 'Emath within its borders'.
findings.after: Both name Emath in connection with borders: Amos sends Israel to Emath Rabba and Geth to see whether these kingdoms' 'borders are greater than your borders', and Zechariah's oracle names 'Emath within its borders'.

findings.finding: The only link is the word 'fowler': a vision of a fowler's vessel and a rhetorical question about a bird falling without a fowler share no image, theme or argument.
Smyrna is not named in the shown text of Revelation 2:10.
findings.before: Both texts speak of being 'tested' for 'ten days': Daniel and his companions are tested in their diet, while the Smyrna believers are told they will be tested and have affliction for ten days.
findings.after: Both texts speak of being 'tested' for 'ten days': Daniel and his companions are tested for ten days, while in Revelation 2:10 believers are told they will be thrown into prison 'that ye may be tested, and ye shall have affliction for ten days.'

findings.finding: 'Fulfilment' does not fit: this is the answer to the king's question within the same scene, not the fulfilment of a prophecy.
findings.before: The king asked Daniel whether he could 'disclose to me the vision I saw and its interpretation', and this verse announces that, having stated 'the vision', Daniel will now give 'its interpretation'.
findings.after: The king asked Daniel whether he could 'disclose to me the vision I saw and its interpretation', and this verse announces that, having stated 'the vision', Daniel will now give 'its interpretation'.

findings.finding: Neither shown text says others had failed, and neither names the king.
findings.before: In both verses Daniel is brought before a king after others have failed: "Daniel was brought before the king" here, and "Arioch urgently brought Daniel to the king" in Daniel 2:25. The kings differ, Baltasar here and Nebuchadnezzar in chapter 2.
findings.after: In both verses Daniel is brought before a king to deal with a hidden matter: 'Daniel was brought before the king' here, and 'Arioch urgently brought Daniel to the king' in Daniel 2:25, presenting him as one 'who will disclose every detail to the king.'

findings.finding: Daniel 11:14 is not a promise; it predicts a rebuilding attempt that will stumble. The remark about 'to establish the prophecy' is speculation presented as support.
findings.before: Both promise that fallen things will be rebuilt: "He will rebuild the fallen things of your nation" here, and "I will rebuild its fallen parts" for David's fallen tent in Amos 9:11. Daniel 11:14 adds "to establish the prophecy," which fits an echo of a promise like this one.
findings.after: Both speak of rebuilding fallen things in nearly the same words: 'He will rebuild the fallen things of your nation' here, and 'I will rebuild its fallen parts' of David's fallen tent in Amos 9:11. In Daniel the one who rebuilds arises 'to establish the prophecy', but they will stumble.

findings.finding: The claim that 'the previous verse says they are already shattered' relies on Ezekiel 30:21, which is not the target text of this pair.
findings.before: Ezekiel 30:22 announces a second shattering: "I will shatter his arms", although the previous verse says they are already shattered. This matches Daniel's "shatter the already-shattered arms." In Ezekiel the arms are Pharaoh's; Daniel's verse does not name whose arms they are.
findings.after: Ezekiel 30:22 announces, 'I will shatter his arms, the strong and the outstretched', the same image as Daniel's 'shatter the already-shattered arms'. In Ezekiel the arms are Pharaoh's; Daniel's verse does not name whose arms they are.

findings.finding: Ecclesiastes 12:4 as shown does not mention death; 'the approach of death' is an interpretation presented as the text's application.
findings.before: Both picture the silencing of ordinary sounds of life, pairing the sound of grinding with the sound of song: Ecclesiastes has "the grinding woman's voice weakens" and "daughters of song are brought low," while Revelation says musicians and "the sound of a mill" will not be heard any more. Revelation applies the image to the fallen city, Ecclesiastes to the approach of death.
findings.after: Both picture the silencing of ordinary sounds of life, pairing the sound of grinding with the sound of song: Ecclesiastes has 'the grinding woman's voice weakens' and 'all the daughters of song are brought low', while Revelation says musicians and 'the sound of a mill' will not be heard any more. Revelation applies the image to the city addressed.

findings.finding: Nehemiah 1:1 as shown does not mention a Persian king.
findings.before: Nehemiah is in Sousan, the same royal city called Susa in Esther, under a Persian king. The spelling differs (Sousan).
findings.after: Nehemiah is in Sousan ('Sousan abira'), the same city called Susa in Esther 1:2, where King Artaxerxes was enthroned. The spelling differs (Sousan).

findings.finding: Neither shown text says what the first letter ordered or that the second counters it.
findings.before: Both introduce the full text of a royal letter of Artaxerxes with "This is/The following is a copy of the letter." The first letter in 3:13a ordered the Jews' destruction; the second, introduced here, counters it.
findings.after: Both introduce the full text of a royal letter with the same formula, 'This is the copy of the letter' / 'The following is a copy of the letter'; in 3:13a the letter opens 'The great King Artaxerxes writes the following to the rulers of the hundred and twenty-seven territories'.

findings.finding: Ezekiel 7:23 does not say the land is filled with lawlessness; it says the land is full of peoples and the city full of lawlessness.
findings.before: Both charge that the land has been filled with lawlessness. Ezekiel 8:17 says the house of Judah 'filled the land with lawlessness', and this unit speaks of the city full of lawlessness.
findings.after: Both speak of fullness of lawlessness: Ezekiel 8:17 says the house of Judah 'filled the land with lawlessness', and this unit says 'the city full of lawlessness'.

findings.finding: The source says 'Those saying, ‘On the Lord’s day,’ did not rise'; the rationale misreads this as the prophets not rising 'on the Lord's day'.
findings.before: Both describe a failure to stand on Israel's behalf at the time of judgment. Here the prophets 'did not stand in a firm position' and did not rise on 'the Lord's day'. In Ezekiel 22:30, God sought a man 'standing wholly before Me at the land's time' but found none. The shared element is the act of standing, not a breach or a wall.
findings.after: Both describe a failure to stand on Israel's behalf at the time of judgment. Here 'they did not stand in a firm position', and 'those saying, ‘On the Lord’s day,’ did not rise'. In Ezekiel 22:30 God sought a man 'standing wholly before Me at the land's time' but found none. The shared element is the act of standing, not a breach or a wall.

findings.finding: The rationale paraphrases Ezekiel 43:15 as horns that 'rise a cubit above the Ariel'. The shown text says 'from the Ariel upward above the horns was a cubit'.
findings.before: Both texts give the altar structure horns, which Exodus places on its four corners and which Ezekiel says rise a cubit above the Ariel. The structure Ezekiel calls the Ariel and its four-cubit height have no counterpart in Exodus.
findings.after: Both texts give the altar horns. Exodus 27:2 places horns on its four corners, of one piece with it and covered with bronze, and Ezekiel 43:15 says that 'from the Ariel upward above the horns was a cubit'. The structure Ezekiel calls the Ariel and its four-cubit height have no counterpart in Exodus.

findings.finding: The rationale says both oracles 'end' with the pairing and that peoples and nations are 'brought to nothing' in both. Habakkuk 2:13 does not close an oracle, and the shown Jeremiah text says 'Peoples will not labor in vain'.
findings.before: Both oracles end with the same pairing of peoples and nations brought to nothing, set beside fire: in Habakkuk peoples fail in fire and nations lose heart, while in Jeremiah Babylon's gates are burned and peoples and nations perish. The wording differs in detail.
findings.after: Both pair peoples and nations with fire in a saying of judgment. Habakkuk has 'Many peoples failed in fire, and many nations lost heart', and in Jeremiah Babylon's 'high gates burned', with 'Peoples will not labor in vain, and nations will perish at the beginning.' The wording differs in detail.

findings.finding: The only shared element is the common phrase 'transgress(ed) covenant', which recurs widely. The shown 2 Kings 18:12 does not name the northern kingdom's fall or otherwise tie itself to Hosea 6:7, so the link rests on a general phrase.
In the shown Hosea 7:1 the robber strips Ephraim ('a robber stripping him on his road'), so the robbery there is done to him. It does not depict Israel's own lawlessness, as the rationale states.
findings.before: Hosea 6:9 gives the people the strength of a pirate and speaks of the Lord's road; Hosea 7:1 describes a robber stripping him on his road. Both use robbery on the road to depict Israel's lawlessness.
findings.after: Both verses use the image of robbery on the road. In Hosea 6:9 the people's strength is 'that of a pirate' and the priests 'concealed the Lord's road'. In Hosea 7:1, where Ephraim's injustice is uncovered because 'they practiced falsehood', 'a robber' strips him 'on his road'.

findings.finding: The pair is labelled verbal echo, but the two verses share no wording ('no one among them calling to Me' against 'did not return to the Lord their God or seek Him'). The link is a repeated charge within the oracle.
findings.before: Hosea 7:7 says there was no one among them calling to Me, and Hosea 7:10 says they did not return to the Lord their God or seek Him. Both verses of the same oracle state that Israel would not turn to God amid its disorders.
findings.after: Hosea 7:7 says there was 'no one among them calling to Me', and Hosea 7:10 says 'they did not return to the Lord their God or seek Him in all these things.' Both verses of the same oracle charge that Israel would not turn to God amid its disorders.

findings.finding: The final sentence reads both similes as pictures of Israel's corruption, but in 10:4 it is 'judgment' that springs up like wild grass.
findings.before: Both verses in Hosea use a simile set upon the field's fallow ground: judgment springs up like wild grass there, and altars are like tortoises there. Each pictures Israel's corruption as something spread over untilled land.
findings.after: Both verses in Hosea use a simile set upon 'the field's fallow ground'. In 10:4 'judgment will spring up like wild grass on the field's fallow ground', and in 12:12 the altars of the rulers sacrificing at Gilgal 'are like tortoises upon the field's fallow ground'.

findings.finding: The shown Hosea 13:2 does not describe calf worship. It speaks of a cast image of silver 'according to the likeness of idols' and of the saying 'calves have run out', which treats calves as sacrifices, not as idols.
findings.before: Hosea 10:5 speaks of the calf beside which Samaria's inhabitants dwell, and Hosea 13:2 describes cast images made from silver and the saying that calves have run out. Both describe Israel's calf worship.
findings.after: Both verses in Hosea condemn Israel's crafted cult images. Hosea 10:5 speaks of 'the calf of the house of On' beside which Samaria's inhabitants dwell, and Hosea 13:2 of 'a cast image from their silver according to the likeness of idols, works completed for them by craftsmen'.

findings.finding: The rationale merges two items. In Isaiah 3:22 the 'coverings used about the house' are not called transparent; the transparent item is the 'Laconian garments'.
findings.before: Isaiah lists coverings used about the house and transparent garments among luxuries, and Esther 1:6 describes transparent coverings adorned with varied flowers in the royal court. Both name transparent coverings as household luxury fabrics.
findings.after: Both name transparent fabrics among luxury goods. Isaiah 3:22 lists 'the coverings used about the house and the transparent Laconian garments', and Esther 1:6 describes 'transparent coverings adorned with varied flowers' among the furnishings of a lavish setting.

findings.finding: Isaiah 7:19 pictures the swarm settling in ravines, holes of the rocks, caves and trees. Jeremiah 16:16 pictures hunters searching people out of the rocks' openings. Beyond the common mention of rock holes there is no specific shared image, and Isaiah 7:19 says nothing of reaching into hiding places, as the rationale claims.

In the shown Zechariah 14:10, 'Rama will remain in its place, from Benjamin's Gate to the place of the First Gate... to the king's wine vats' gives the extent of Jerusalem itself, marked by its gates. It is not the town of Rama north of Jerusalem, so the rationale's identification is unsupported. The shown Isaiah 10:29 also has no Gabe.

Isaiah 37:22 is not addressed to Zion and Jerusalem. It is a word 'concerning him' in which daughter Zion and daughter Jerusalem respond to him, so 'address Zion and Jerusalem together' and the label 'parallel address' do not fit.
findings.before: Isaiah 10:32 names Daughter Zion and the hills in Jerusalem, and Isaiah 37:22 names virgin daughter Zion and daughter Jerusalem responding to the Assyrian king. Both address Zion and Jerusalem together in the face of the Assyrian threat.
findings.after: Both name Daughter Zion together with Jerusalem. Isaiah 10:32 speaks of 'the mountain, Daughter Zion, and the hills in Jerusalem', and in Isaiah 37:22 'Virgin daughter Zion despised and sneered at you; daughter Jerusalem shook her head over you.' Both belong to Isaiah's oracles on the Assyrian threat to Jerusalem.

findings.finding: The quotation 'the Lord delivered over to our sins' is not in the target, which reads 'the Lord delivered him over to our sins'.
findings.before: Both passages in the same song speak of the same afflicted figure and of the Lord acting toward him: earlier he is 'a man under affliction' whom 'the Lord delivered over to our sins', and here 'the Lord desires to cleanse him of his affliction'. The two describe different divine actions toward his affliction.
findings.after: Both passages in the same song speak of the same afflicted figure and of the Lord acting toward him. Earlier he is 'a man under affliction' and 'the Lord delivered him over to our sins'; here 'the Lord desires to cleanse him of his affliction'. The two describe different divine actions toward his affliction.

findings.finding: Nehemiah 9:32 speaks of the 'hardship' of kings, rulers, priests and prophets, not their failure. The confession of failure in 9:34 names kings, rulers, priests and fathers, without prophets.
findings.before: Nehemiah 9:32-34 confesses the failure of "our kings, rulers, priests, prophets" and all the people, matching the list of kings, rulers, priests and prophets who will be ashamed in Jeremiah 2:26.
findings.after: Nehemiah 9:32 names the hardship of 'our kings, rulers, priests, prophets, fathers and all Thy people', and 9:34 confesses that 'Our kings, rulers, priests and fathers did not carry out Thy law'. The same classes of leaders (kings, rulers, priests and prophets) are those who will be ashamed in Jeremiah 2:26.

findings.finding: The shared elements are only 'all' and 'lawless' in a general charge of universal guilt. That is a common theme, not a specific verbal echo.
Jeremiah 3:16 places the ark's passing from mind 'in those days', a future time, not 'in Jeremiah's time'. 2 Maccabees 2:5 speaks of a 'cave-like chamber', not simply a cave.
findings.before: Both concern the ark in Jeremiah's time passing out of use. Jeremiah 3:16 says the ark of the covenant will not be attended to or made again, and 2 Maccabees 2:5 tells how Jeremiah hid the ark in a cave and blocked the entrance.
findings.after: Both concern the ark of the covenant. Jeremiah 3:16 says that in those days the ark 'will not come to mind, be named or be attended to, and it will not be made again', and 2 Maccabees 2:5 tells how Jeremiah brought the tent, the ark and the altar of incense into a cave-like chamber and blocked the entrance.

findings.finding: The rationale refers to 'the corruption of prophets and priests that this announcement introduces', which is not in the shown Jeremiah 5:30.
findings.before: Both use "horrifying things" for wrongdoing among God's people. Jeremiah 23:14 places them among Jerusalem's prophets, which matches the corruption of prophets and priests that this announcement introduces.
findings.after: Both use the expression 'horrifying things' for wrongdoing among God's people. Jeremiah 5:30 says 'Astonishment and horrifying things happened upon the land', and Jeremiah 23:14 says 'among Jerusalem's prophets I have seen horrifying things'.

findings.finding: In the shown Jeremiah 6:7, 'continually before her' refers to impiety and misery, and 'With pain and scourging' begins a new clause. The text does not pair continual pain with scourging, as the rationale states.
findings.before: Both pair continual pain with scourging: misery "continually before her. With pain and scourging" and "I am ready for scourges, and my pain is continually before me."
findings.after: Both set something 'continually before' the subject next to pain and scourging. In Jeremiah impiety and misery are heard in her, 'continually before her. With pain and scourging', and in the psalm 'I am ready for scourges, and my pain is continually before me.'

findings.finding: Habakkuk 1:3 does not place the impiety and misery in a city, as the rationale implies.
findings.before: Both use the paired words impiety and misery for the wrongdoing seen in the city. Jeremiah says "impiety and misery will be heard in her", and Habakkuk complains of having to look upon "misery and impiety."
findings.after: Both use the paired words impiety and misery for wrongdoing. Jeremiah says 'impiety and misery will be heard in her', and Habakkuk complains of having 'to look upon misery and impiety'.

findings.finding: The shared elements are only 'see' and the common phrase 'Jerusalem's streets'. The passages make different points: one searches for a man doing justice, the other points to what is being done in the streets.
Rationale says both texts show 'failed warriors', but the source says only 'his warriors are going out'.
findings.before: Both describe the fall of Babylon in the same oracle with burning and failed warriors. Her "gatherings were burned with fire" and "her dwellings were burned", while "his warriors are going out" and "Babylon's warrior has ceased fighting."
findings.after: Both describe Babylon's fall in the same oracle with burning and with its warriors: 'their gatherings were burned with fire' and 'Her dwellings were burned', while 'his warriors are going out' and 'Babylon's warrior has ceased fighting.'

findings.finding: The rationale says the 'Assyrian envoy' boasts that 'their gods could not rescue them', and calls the cities 'Syrian'. None of this is in the shown texts. The verse shown asks whether they rescued Samaria.
findings.before: Both name the Syrian cities Hamath and Arpad together, spelled Aimath and Arphad in 2 Kings 18:34. There the Assyrian envoy boasts that their gods could not rescue them, while Jeremiah says they were ashamed at an evil report.
findings.after: Both name Hamath and Arpad together, spelled Aimath and Arphad in 2 Kings 18:34. There the speaker asks, 'Where is the god of Aimath and Arphad?' and whether they rescued Samaria from his hand. Jeremiah says Hamath and Arpad were ashamed because they heard an evil report.

findings.finding: The target shows the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim being asked to bring up the ark. It does not show them receiving it.
findings.before: Both name the town of Kiriath-jearim, whose inhabitants received the returned ark. The link concerns the town only and does not identify Uriah son of Shemaiah.
findings.after: Both name the town of Kiriath-jearim, whose inhabitants were summoned to come down and bring up the returned ark of the Lord. The link concerns the town only and does not identify Uriah son of Shemaiah.

findings.finding: The shown target does not say Zephaniah was the recipient of 'the same letter'. It only directs a message to him.
findings.before: The Zephaniah who reads the document in Jeremiah's hearing is the Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest named in the same letter as its recipient.
findings.after: The Zephaniah who reads the document in Jeremiah's hearing is Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, to whom the message in Jeremiah 36:25 is directed: 'And to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest say.'

findings.finding: The source does not picture Israel returning toward Zion. Zion is addressed, and Israel is told to turn back 'to your cities'.
findings.before: Both picture Israel taking the way back toward Zion. The source tells Zion and virgin Israel to turn back along the road they traveled, and the other passage says they will ask the way as far as Zion and turn their faces there.
findings.after: Both picture exiled Israel on the road of return. The source tells virgin Israel to turn back along the road she traveled, to her cities, and Jeremiah 27:5 says they will ask the way as far as Zion and turn their faces there.

findings.finding: Jeremiah 51:12-14 is a later oracle that announces the punishment. It does not record the punishment being carried out, so 'fulfillment' and 'carries out' are inaccurate.
findings.before: Jeremiah 51:12-14 announces punishment on Judah's survivors 'residing in Egypt's land' by sword and famine. This carries out the warning against going to live in Egypt.
findings.after: Jeremiah 51:12-14 announces punishment on Judah's remainder 'residing in Egypt's land': they will perish by sword and famine, and none will be saved to return. This is the judgment threatened by the warning 'If you set your faces toward Egypt and go in to live there.'

findings.finding: The claim that 'in each case his hearers immediately turn on him' goes beyond the source as shown. Jeremiah 50:1 shows only the opening clause.
findings.before: Both begin with Jeremiah stopping speaking the words the Lord gave him for the people: 'when Jeremiah stopped speaking everything the Lord commanded him to speak to all the people.' In each case his hearers immediately turn on him.
findings.after: Both begin with the same formula for Jeremiah finishing the Lord's words to the people: 'When Jeremiah stopped speaking to the people all the Lord's words' and 'when Jeremiah stopped speaking everything the Lord commanded him to speak to all the people.'

findings.finding: 'This will be the sign for you' is a common formula, and there is no other specific link between the two passages. The rationale also says the source's sign is 'the handing over of Egypt's king', which is not in the shown source.
The only shared word is 'trembling'. The rationale's 'message spoken to him by a visitor' is not in the shown source (Job 4:14).
'Desert peoples' and 'trading peoples' are not in the shown texts.
findings.before: Teman is listed beside Dedan among the desert peoples in Jeremiah 32:23. This matches the trading peoples whose roads Job names together with the Sabeans.
findings.after: Jeremiah 32:23 names Teman beside Dedan and Ros. Job 6:19 points to the roads of the Temanites, the people of the same place.

findings.finding: 'Rescue ... from the hand of' is a common idiom, and the contexts are unrelated (Job's sarcastic question to his friends, and God's promise to Jeremiah). There is no specific connection.
The link rests on the common word 'righteous' and on reading 'the righteous person' in Job 6:29 as Job himself, which the shown text does not establish.
The two comparisons differ ('lighter than chatter' and 'swifter than a runner'), so it is not 'the same comparison'. Only the form is shared, and the source does not explicitly speak of speed.
findings.before: Job uses the same comparison for how quickly his life passes: 'My life is lighter than chatter' and 'My life is swifter than a runner.'
findings.after: Job uses the same form of comparison for his fleeting life: 'My life is lighter than chatter' and 'My life is swifter than a runner.'

findings.finding: 'Strength' and 'not spare' are common words used in unrelated contexts (Job on his own speech, and the Lord commissioning the prophet to denounce sins). The match is coincidental vocabulary.
The rationale says that in 12:5 'Job speaks of himself', but the shown target speaks of 'he'.
findings.before: Bildad's 'an extraordinary fall has been prepared for him' echoes Job's earlier words that 'he was prepared to fall beneath others'. Both use the language of someone being prepared for a fall, but Job speaks of himself, and Bildad speaks of the wicked man.
findings.after: Bildad's 'An extraordinary fall has been prepared for him' echoes Job's earlier words that 'he was prepared to fall beneath others'. Both speak of a man prepared for a fall: in Job 12:5 one whose houses are plundered by the lawless, in Bildad's speech the man under judgment.

findings.finding: 'My eye has seen' is a common phrase, and here it has different objects (what Job has seen in general in 13:1, and what he will know within himself in 19:27). There is no specific connection.
The rationale asserts that these are the only two places the heading occurs, which cannot be checked from the two texts shown.
findings.before: The heading 'Job continued and said in his prelude:' is repeated word for word at chapter 29. These are the only two places where it introduces Job's continuing discourse.
findings.after: The heading 'Job continued and said in his prelude:' is repeated word for word at chapter 29, introducing Job's continuing discourse again.

findings.finding: The rationale quotes 31:28 ('before the Lord Most High'), which is neither the source nor the target, and says Job's text concerns turning the heart from God, which the shown verse does not state.
findings.before: Both concern a secret deception that would turn the heart from God. Job disavows having his heart 'secretly deceived' (31:28 adds that it would mean lying 'before the Lord Most High'), and Deuteronomy warns of anyone who 'entices you secretly' to serve other gods.
findings.after: Both speak of a secret deception connected with false worship. Job disavows that his heart was 'secretly deceived' or that he 'placed my hand upon my mouth and kissed it', and Deuteronomy warns of anyone who 'entices you secretly, saying: Let us go and serve other gods'.

findings.finding: Only a general theme of Job wanting a hearing; 'someone who hears me' and 'I will argue before Him' share no distinctive wording or image, and 31:35 does not name God as the hearer.
Addressing hearers as wise is a common form of address, not a specific link; the rationale also relies on a quotation ('Let us choose judgment for ourselves') that appears in neither shown text.
The rationale says both texts use 'travel' 'on a road', but 'on a road' occurs only in Sirach; Job has 'sharing a road' and 'to travel with the ungodly'.
findings.before: Both use the phrase 'travel' 'on a road' with a bad companion: here the ungodly, in Sirach a reckless person whom one should not travel with.
findings.after: Both picture keeping company on the road with bad people: Job speaks of 'sharing a road with those doing lawless things, to travel with the ungodly', and Sirach warns 'Do not travel on a road with a reckless person'.

findings.finding: The rationale describes Nehemiah 3:34 as 'a mocking question before the strength of Somoron', but in the shown text 'the strength of Somoron' is part of the question itself.
findings.before: Both texts are hostile reactions by the neighbouring authorities to 'the Jews' who are 'building' the 'city' of Jerusalem: here a mocking question before the strength of Somoron, in Ezra an accusation to the king that the Jews are building the rebellious city.
findings.after: Both texts are hostile reactions to 'the Jews' who are 'building' their 'city': here the mocking question 'Is this the strength of Somoron, that these Jews are building their own city?', and in Ezra an accusation to the king that the Jews 'are building the rebellious and wicked city'.

findings.finding: The rationale says both texts describe a public reading of the book, but neither shown verse narrates a reading: Nehemiah 8:5 has Esdras opening the book, and 2 Kings 23:3 the king making a covenant.
findings.before: Both texts describe a public reading of the book of the law before the assembled nation in which 'all the people stood': here when Esdras opened the book, and in 2 Kings when the king made the covenant from the things written in the book.
findings.after: Both describe the assembled people standing in connection with the book of the law: here 'all the people stood' when Esdras opened the book before them, and in 2 Kings 'All the people stood in the covenant' when the king made the covenant upholding 'the things written in this book'.

findings.finding: The rationale says both lists begin with Saraia, but the shown Nehemiah 10:3 reads 'son of Saraia, and Azaria and Jermia', so it does not begin a list with Saraia.
findings.before: Both are lists of priests that begin with Saraia and include Jermia (here Saraia, Azaria and Jermia; there Saraia, Jermia, Esdra), the names of the priestly houses.
findings.after: Saraia and Jermia appear in both lists of priestly names: here 'son of Saraia, and Azaria and Jermia', and in Nehemiah 12:1 'Saraia, Jermia, Esdra' among the priests and Levites who came up with Zorobabel.

findings.finding: The rationale says both contrast 'human gain' with what comes from the Lord, but 29:26 speaks of courting leaders' favour, not gain.
findings.before: Both sayings contrast human gain with what comes from the Lord: here all righteous things are from the Lord, and in 29:26 what is just for a man comes from the Lord.
findings.after: Both sayings set what people obtain or seek against what comes from the Lord, in closely similar words: here everything comes into the laps of the unjust, but all righteous things are from the Lord, and in 29:26 many court the faces of leaders, but what is just for a man comes from the Lord.

findings.finding: The rationale says both contrast where the wise person's and the fool's eyes are directed, but Proverbs speaks of the wise man's face, not his eyes, and Ecclesiastes says the fool walks in darkness, not where his eyes are.
findings.before: Both contrast where the wise person's and the fool's eyes are directed. Here the fool's eyes are upon the extremities of the earth, and in Ecclesiastes the wise person's eyes are in his head while the fool walks in darkness.
findings.after: Both contrast the wise person and the fool by the face or eyes: here an understanding face belongs to a wise man while the fool's eyes are upon the extremities of the earth, and in Ecclesiastes the wise person's eyes are in his head while the fool walks in darkness.

findings.finding: The connection rests on ruling and lending appearing together, but the teachings differ, so 'shared teaching' does not fit. Also, 'Israel' is not named in the Deuteronomy text shown, which says 'you'.
findings.before: Both pair ruling with lending: here the rich rule the poor and household servants lend to their masters, and in Deuteronomy Israel will lend to many nations and rule over them. The relationship differs: in Proverbs the lenders are servants, while in Deuteronomy they are the rulers.
findings.after: Both pair ruling with lending: here the rich rule the poor and household servants lend to their own masters, and in Deuteronomy those addressed will lend to many nations and not borrow, and will rule over many nations. The roles differ: in Proverbs the lenders are servants, while in Deuteronomy the lenders are the ones who rule.

findings.finding: The rationale says both have young eagles feeding on human remains, but in 24:22e the bones are inedible to the young eagles, so they do not feed.
findings.before: Both use young eagles feeding on human remains in a context of punishment. Here bones are burned so that they are inedible to young eagles, and in 30:17 young eagles devour the eye that mocks a parent.
findings.after: Both mention young eagles in connection with eating what is left of a person under judgment or curse: here bones are burned so that they are inedible to young eagles, and in 30:17 young eagles are to devour the eye that mocks a father and dishonors a mother.

findings.finding: The rationale says the Proverbs verse speaks of paths that leave no knowable trace, but the verse shown only lists the tracks and paths. It does not say they leave no trace.
findings.before: Both use the passing of a ship and the flight of an eagle as examples of a path that leaves no knowable trace: here the tracks of a flying eagle and the paths of a seagoing ship, and in Job the trace of a ship's way or of a flying eagle.
findings.after: Both put the flight of an eagle beside the course of a ship: here the tracks of a flying eagle and the paths of a seagoing ship, and in Job the question whether there is a trace of a ship's way or of an eagle flying in search of food.

findings.finding: The rationale calls Isaiah 24:2 'Isaiah's judgment', but the verse shown does not mention judgment.
findings.before: Both use the maidservant and her mistress as an example of overturned social order. Here a maidservant casts out her own mistress, and in Isaiah's judgment the maidservant will be like the mistress.
findings.after: Both use the maidservant and her mistress as an example of the usual order between them overturned or leveled: here a maidservant casts out her own mistress, and in Isaiah the maidservant will be like the mistress, alongside the slave like the master.

findings.finding: The rationale says Jude calls 'false members' clouds, but the Jude text shown does not call them false. It calls them 'These' at the love feasts.
findings.before: Both liken false people to clouds driven by winds: Proverbs compares those who boast of a false gift to winds and clouds and very conspicuous rains, and Jude calls false members waterless clouds carried along by winds. Proverbs speaks of conspicuous rains while Jude stresses that the clouds are waterless.
findings.after: Both liken people to clouds and winds: Proverbs compares those who boast of a false gift to winds and clouds and very conspicuous rains, and Jude calls those feasting at the love feasts and shepherding themselves waterless clouds carried along by winds. Proverbs speaks of conspicuous rains, while Jude stresses that the clouds are waterless.

findings.finding: The rationale says both bring harmful consequences on the guarantor, but 19:28 says the guarantor treats just judgment with insolence. It does not describe harm to him.
findings.before: Both warn about one who acts as guarantor for an unworthy person: for a man charged with murder in one saying and for a foolish child in the other, with harmful consequences for the guarantor.
findings.after: Both judge harshly one who acts as guarantor for an unworthy person, a man charged with murder in one saying and a foolish child in the other: the first will be a fugitive and not secure, and the second treats just judgment with insolence.

findings.finding: The rationale says both describe murderous people hating the righteous, but 1 John does not say that Cain hated his brother. It speaks of the world hating the brothers.
findings.before: Both describe murderous people hating the righteous: Proverbs says men sharing in bloodshed will hate a holy person, and 1 John says Cain slaughtered his brother because his own works were evil but his brother's were righteous, adding that the world hates believers.
findings.after: Both link bloodshed with hostility toward the righteous: Proverbs says men sharing in bloodshed will hate a holy person, and 1 John says Cain slaughtered his brother because his own works were evil but his brother's were righteous, then tells the brothers not to be surprised if the world hates them.

findings.finding: The link is only the general wish that enemies be shamed, which is common in the psalms. The rationale also claims shared wording 'put to shame together', but Psalm 6:11 has no 'together', and the specific pairing of shame with trouble is missing from 34:26.
The rationale says 7:18 closes Psalm 7, which the texts shown do not establish.
findings.before: Both vow to sing praise to the name of the Most High in nearly identical wording, closing Psalm 7 and opening the praise of Psalm 9.
findings.after: Both vow to sing praise to the name of the Most High in nearly identical wording: sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High, and I will sing praise to Thy name, Most High.

findings.finding: The rationale speaks of God bringing down 'enemies', but Sirach 10:17 does not call those removed enemies.
findings.before: Both describe God bringing down enemies so that their memory ends: their memory perished, and He made their memory cease from the earth.
findings.after: Both describe people brought down so that their memory ends: here Thou didst pull down cities and their memory perished with a noise, and in Sirach He removed some and destroyed them, and made their memory cease from the earth.

findings.finding: The rationale says Ezekiel's words are 'said to the ruler of Tyre', but Tyre is not named in the text shown.
findings.before: Both insist that proud powers must recognize they are merely human: let nations know that they are human beings, and You are a human, and not a god, said to the ruler of Tyre.
findings.after: Both insist that the proud must recognize they are merely human: let nations know that they are human beings, and You are a human, and not a god, said to one who would claim, 'I am a god.'

findings.finding: The rationale calls these 'hostile nations' that are 'not divine', but the Isaiah text does not present the Egyptian as hostile, and the psalm does not say 'not divine'.
findings.before: Both stress that hostile nations are human beings and not divine: let nations know that they are human beings, and an Egyptian human being and not God.
findings.after: Both stress that nations are merely human: let nations know that they are human beings, and an Egyptian human being and not God, against whom the Lord will bring His hand.

findings.finding: The rationale says Deuteronomy recalls what God did 'for Israel in Egypt', but neither Israel nor Egypt is named in the text shown.
findings.before: Both pair God seeing the sufferer's 'humiliation' with his 'toil': 'See my humiliation and my toil' and 'the Lord ... saw our humiliation, and our toil'. Deuteronomy recalls what God did for Israel in Egypt, while the psalm asks God to do this now and also asks forgiveness for all sins.
findings.after: Both pair God seeing the sufferer's 'humiliation' with his 'toil': 'See my humiliation and my toil' and 'the Lord ... saw our humiliation, and our toil'. Deuteronomy recalls what the Lord did when 'we cried unto the Lord, the God of our fathers', while the psalm asks God to see now and also asks forgiveness for all sins.

findings.finding: The rationale names Jacob as the speaker, but the text shown does not name him.
findings.before: Both speak of God seeing the speaker's humiliation and toil: 'See my humiliation and my toil' and 'God saw my humiliation and the toil of my hands'. Jacob states what God has already done, while the psalm asks God to see and adds a plea for forgiveness.
findings.after: Both speak of God seeing the speaker's humiliation and toil: 'See my humiliation and my toil' and 'God saw my humiliation and the toil of my hands'. The Genesis speaker states what God has already done, while the psalm asks God to see and adds a plea for forgiveness.

findings.finding: The rationale says both laments 'end with' the plea, but the texts shown do not show either verse to be a closing verse.
findings.before: Both laments end with the same plea to the Lord: do not depart from me. Psalm 37 pairs it with do not abandon me, while Psalm 34 pairs it with do not remain silent.
findings.after: Both laments contain the same plea to the Lord: do not depart from me. Psalm 37 pairs it with do not abandon me, while Psalm 34 pairs it with do not remain silent.

findings.finding: The verbs differ (praised and glorified), so 'verbal echo' overstates the match.
findings.before: Both state in the passive what God's people will receive in God: in God we will be praised, and in God they will be glorified, said of Israel's offspring.
findings.after: Both state in the passive what will come to God's people in God: in God we will be praised, and in God they will be glorified, said of all the offspring of Israel's sons.

findings.finding: The rationale says Psalm 119's arrows are aimed 'against a deceitful tongue', but the verse shown does not mention a tongue.
findings.before: Both use the phrase of the mighty one's sharpened arrows. In Psalm 44 the arrows strike the king's enemies, while in Psalm 119 they are paired with desert coals against a deceitful tongue.
findings.after: Both use the phrase of the mighty one's sharpened arrows. In Psalm 44 the arrows strike the heart of the king's enemies, while in Psalm 119 they are paired with desert coals.

findings.finding: The rationale speaks of 'the mighty king', but in 2 Samuel the mighty one is the Lord and the speaker is not named as king.
findings.before: Both describe peoples being brought beneath the mighty king. Psalm 44 says peoples will fall beneath you, and 2 Samuel 22 says the mighty Lord disciplines peoples beneath me.
findings.after: Both describe peoples brought beneath the one favored by the mighty one: Psalm 44 says to the mighty one, peoples will fall beneath you, and in 2 Samuel the mighty Lord disciplines peoples beneath me.

findings.finding: The rationale says both picture young women with the bride being brought to the king and calls both 'royal love songs'. In the Song, the young women are not brought to the king; the speaker is.
findings.before: Both royal love songs picture young women with the bride and her being brought to the king. Psalm 44 says virgins behind her will be brought to the king, and the Song says young women loved you and the king brought me into his chamber.
findings.after: Both join young women with a woman brought to the king: Psalm 44 says virgins behind her will be brought to the king and her companions brought unto you, and in the Song young women loved you and the king brought me into his chamber.

findings.finding: The rationale says 'Both ask', but the psalm declares; it does not ask.
findings.before: Both ask whether the Lord receives calves as offerings. God declares, I will not receive calves from your house, and Micah asks whether the Lord will receive year-old calves and thousands of rams, then names what the Lord seeks instead.
findings.after: Both concern whether the Lord accepts calves as offerings: God declares, I will not receive calves from your house, and Micah asks whether the Lord is to be grasped with year-old calves or received with thousands of rams, then names what the Lord seeks instead.

findings.finding: The rationale says both verses 'end with' the vow, but in Psalm 51:11 it comes at the beginning of the verse.
findings.before: Both end with the same vow, I will thank Thee for ever. Psalm 51 gives the reason because Thou didst act, while Psalm 29 addresses Lord my God.
findings.after: Both contain the same vow, I will thank Thee for ever. Psalm 51 gives the reason because Thou didst act, while Psalm 29 addresses Lord my God.

findings.finding: The rationale compares 'twelve thousand' with Samuel's twenty-two thousand Syrians, but in the heading the twelve thousand belong to Joab's strike in the Valley of Salt, not to the Syrian campaign.
findings.before: The heading's campaign against Syria Zobah matches the war against Hadadezer king of Zobah, in which Syrians are struck down. The agent and count differ: the heading names Joab and twelve thousand, Samuel names David and twenty-two thousand Syrians.
findings.after: The heading's campaign against Syria Zobah corresponds to the war in which Syria of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah and David struck down twenty-two thousand Syrian men. The heading's twelve thousand belong to Joab's separate strike in the Valley of Salt.

findings.finding: The rationale calls the commanders 'a general of David's house', but David is not named in either text shown.
findings.before: Both record a slaughter in the Valley of Salt (Valley of Salts) by a general of David's house. The heading names Joab and twelve thousand, while Chronicles names Abessa son of Sarouia and eighteen thousand of Idumea.
findings.after: Both record a slaughter in the Valley of Salt (Valley of Salts): the heading says Joab struck the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand, and Chronicles says Abessa son of Sarouia struck Idumea in the Valley of Salts, eighteen thousand.

findings.finding: The rationale speaks of 'spoils of war shared beyond the fighters', but the psalm verse shown does not mention war or fighters.
findings.before: Both have spoils of war shared beyond the fighters: for the beauty of the house to divide spoils, and divide the spoils between the warriors and the whole congregation.
findings.after: Both speak of dividing spoils with a share beyond those who fought: in the psalm spoils are divided for the beauty of the house, and in Numbers the spoils are divided between the warriors who go forth into battle and the whole congregation.

findings.finding: The rationale says the psalm verse is 'in God's procession' and calls Judges 5 'the song of victory', but neither is stated in the texts shown.
findings.before: Zebulun and Naphtali are named together in both, here among the rulers in God's procession and in Judges in the song of victory.
findings.after: Zebulun and Naphtali are named together in both: Zebulun's rulers and Naphtali's rulers in the psalm, and in Judges Zebulun, a people that scorned its life to the point of death, and Naphtali on the heights of the field.

findings.finding: The rationale says Benjamin's whole tribe is called the smallest, but Saul calls his clan the smallest within Benjamin, and Benjamin is 'Israel's small tribal division'.
findings.before: Benjamin is singled out as the lesser tribe: Benjamin, the younger, and Benjamin's whole tribe as the smallest.
findings.after: Benjamin is singled out as small: Benjamin, the younger, in the psalm, and Saul's description of Benjamin as Israel's small tribal division, with his own clan the smallest in it.

findings.finding: The rationale speaks of God's majesty 'toward Israel', but Deuteronomy 33:26 as shown does not name Israel. It speaks of the God of the beloved.
findings.before: God's majesty toward Israel is located in the heavens: His magnificence is over Israel and His power in the clouds, and the God of the beloved rides upon heaven, the majestic One of the firmament.
findings.after: Both locate God's majesty in the heavens on behalf of His people: His magnificence is over Israel and His power in the clouds, and the God of the beloved rides upon heaven as your helper, the majestic One of the firmament.

findings.finding: The rationale calls this a 'royal psalm' in which 'the king' saves, but the verses shown say only 'He'.
findings.before: Within the same royal psalm the king saves the needy: save the souls of the needy, and save the children of the needy, both alongside care for the poor.
findings.after: Within the same psalm He saves the needy: save the souls of the needy, and save the children of the needy, both alongside care for the poor.

findings.finding: The rationale says 72:7 is 'followed by they spoke', but that wording is in 72:8 and not in the source shown. The idea that fat stands for 'insensibility' is also not stated in the texts.
findings.before: In both, fat stands for the wicked's insensibility, linked to their speech: injustice will come out as though from fat, followed by they spoke, and they shut up their fat; their mouth spoke arrogance.
findings.after: In both, fat is linked to the wicked's wrongdoing: their injustice will come out as though from fat, and they shut up their fat; their mouth spoke arrogance.

findings.finding: The rationale calls the person 'the arrogant wicked person', but neither text as shown says arrogant, and Job 15:27 as shown does not call him wicked.
findings.before: The arrogant wicked person is characterized by fat in both: injustice coming out as though from fat, and he covered his face with his fat.
findings.after: Both describe the people in view by their fat: their injustice will come out as though from fat, and he covered his face with his fat and made a collar upon his thighs.

findings.finding: The rationale names 'the false prophets addressed in Jeremiah' and says they oppose God, but neither appears in the text shown.
findings.before: Both describe God placing lasting disgrace on those who oppose Him: He gave them everlasting reproach here, and I will put eternal reproach upon you in Jeremiah. The recipients differ (God's enemies versus the false prophets addressed in Jeremiah).
findings.after: Both describe God placing lasting reproach on people: He gave them everlasting reproach here, and I will put eternal reproach and eternal dishonor upon you in Jeremiah. The recipients differ: His enemies here, and those addressed as 'you' in Jeremiah.

findings.finding: The rationale says the victim is 'the vine' and calls Jeremiah's victims 'God's people', but neither is stated in the texts shown.
findings.before: Both picture wild animals coming out of the woodland to ravage God's people: a pig from the woodland ravaged her here, and a lion from the woodland struck them in Jeremiah. The animals differ (pig and solitary wild beast versus lion, wolf and leopard), and here the victim is the vine.
findings.after: Both picture wild animals from the woodland ravaging: a pig from the woodland ravaged her here, and a lion from the woodland struck them in Jeremiah. The animals differ: a pig and a solitary wild beast here, a lion, wolf and leopard in Jeremiah.

findings.finding: The rationale says Israel made war and calls the Hagarenes hostile to Israel, but neither text as shown names Israel or states hostility.
findings.before: The Hagarenes appear in both as a people hostile to Israel. Here their dwellings are listed with the Idumeans, Ishmaelites and Moab, and in Chronicles Israel made war against the Hagarenes and the Hagaraeans and all their tents were given into their hands. The Chronicles war is not shown to be the same coalition.
findings.after: The Hagarenes are named in both: here their dwellings are listed with the Idumeans, Ishmaelites and Moab, and in Chronicles they made war against the Hagarenes, and the Hagaraeans and all their tents were given into their hands. The Chronicles war is not shown to involve the same coalition.

findings.finding: The rationale names 'Israel's hostile neighbours' and 'the peoples David plundered', but neither Israel nor David is named in the texts shown.
findings.before: Both list the same group of Israel's hostile neighbours: Ammon, Amalek and the foreigners here, and the sons of Ammon, the foreigners and Amalek among the peoples David plundered in 2 Samuel. Gebal and Tyre are not in the 2 Samuel list.
findings.after: Both lists name Ammon, Amalek and the foreigners: Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, and foreigners here, and the sons of Ammon, the foreigners, Amalek in 2 Samuel, alongside the spoil of Hadadezer. Gebal and Tyre are not in the 2 Samuel list.

findings.finding: The source does not speak of God judging; it speaks of disciplining nations and rebuking. Only Job mentions judging.
findings.before: Both ask a rhetorical question about God as teacher of knowledge who also judges: the One who teaches humankind knowledge here, and Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge? He Himself will judge, in Job.
findings.after: Both ask a rhetorical question about God as the teacher of knowledge: 'the One who teaches humankind knowledge' here, and 'Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?' in Job. Here the same One disciplines nations and rebukes; in Job He will judge murders.

findings.finding: The shown Matthew text does not name the speaker as the Lord; it has only 'I'.
findings.before: Both join not knowing an evildoer with separation from him: the evil one turned away from me, I did not know him here, and I never knew you. Depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness in Matthew. In Matthew the Lord orders them to depart; here the evil one turned away.
findings.after: Both join not knowing an evildoer with separation from him: 'when the evil one turned away from me, I did not know him' here, and 'I never knew you. Depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness' in Matthew. In Matthew the speaker orders them to depart; here the evil one turned away.

findings.finding: The source verse does not say its nesting place was made by God, and 'creation psalm' is a characterization not given in the shown texts.
findings.before: In the same creation psalm, birds will nest in the places God has made: the birds of heaven will nest here, and there sparrows will nest in the cedars He planted. The voice from the rocks here has no counterpart in that verse.
findings.after: Within the same psalm, birds are said to nest: 'the birds of heaven will nest' upon them here, and 'there sparrows will nest' in the cedars of Lebanon that He planted in Psalms 103:17. The voice from the rocks here has no counterpart in that verse.

findings.finding: The rationale reads 'from the Lord' as saying the slanderers' work is from the Lord, an interpretation the verse does not state.
findings.before: Both describe the same kind of adversaries: those slandering me ... those speaking evil against my soul here, and those slandering my soul ... those seeking evil for me in Psalms 70. Psalms 70 asks for their shame, while this verse speaks of their work as from the Lord.
findings.after: Both describe the same kind of adversaries: 'those slandering me ... those speaking evil against my soul' here, and 'those slandering my soul ... those seeking evil for me' in Psalms 70. Psalms 70 asks that they be ashamed and fail; this verse speaks of 'the work of those slandering me, from the Lord'.

findings.finding: The claim that the idea is 'rare' is not supported by the texts, and 1 Chronicles 28:9 as shown speaks of serving and seeking God, not of keeping His commands.
findings.before: Both texts use the rare idea of being forsaken 'utterly' in connection with keeping God's commands. 1 Chronicles 28:9 warns that whoever forsakes God will be forsaken utterly, while the psalmist resolves 'I will keep Thine ordinances' and asks 'do not forsake me utterly.'
findings.after: Both texts speak of being forsaken 'utterly': the psalmist resolves 'I will keep Thine ordinances' and asks 'do not forsake me utterly', while 1 Chronicles 28:9 warns 'if you forsake Him, He will forsake you utterly' after urging Solomon to serve God and seek Him.

findings.finding: Psalms 18:12 says the servant 'keeps them'; it does not mention God's words.
findings.before: Both texts link God's servant, keeping God's words, and recompense. The psalmist asks 'Recompense Thy servant' and promises to keep the words, and Psalms 18:12 states that 'Thy servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great recompense.'
findings.after: Both texts link Thy servant, keeping, and recompense. The psalmist asks 'Recompense Thy servant' and promises to 'keep Thy words', and Psalms 18:12 states 'Thy servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great recompense.'

findings.finding: The wording is similar, not the same: 'compassions' / 'mercy' and 'come to' / 'come upon'.
findings.before: Both verses ask that God's kindness come to the speaker, using the same wording: 'Let Thy compassions come to me' and 'May Thy mercy also come upon me.'
findings.after: Both verses ask that God's kindness come to the speaker, in similar wording: 'Let Thy compassions come to me' and 'May Thy mercy also come upon me.'

findings.finding: Psalms 118:51 does not say the arrogant acted lawlessly against the speaker.
findings.before: Both verses describe 'the arrogant' acting lawlessly against the speaker and then state his loyalty to God's instruction. Here he will ponder the commandments, and in Psalms 118:51 he did not turn from the law.
findings.after: Both verses describe 'the arrogant' acting lawlessly and then state the speaker's loyalty to God's instruction. Here they acted lawlessly against him and he will ponder the commandments; in Psalms 118:51 they acted lawlessly 'to an extreme' and he did not turn away from the law.

findings.finding: Psalms 118:45 applies 'broad' to a place, not to the commandments, so the opening statement is inaccurate.
findings.before: Both verses apply the word 'broad' to the commandments. The source calls God's commandment 'exceedingly broad', and Psalms 118:45 speaks of walking 'in a broad place' because the speaker sought the commandments.
findings.after: Both verses join the word 'broad' to God's commandments: the source calls God's commandment 'exceedingly broad', and Psalms 118:45 speaks of walking 'in a broad place' because the speaker sought the commandments.

findings.finding: The quoted word 'longing' appears in neither verse; both use 'longed'.
findings.before: Both verses describe the speaker's 'longing' directed at God's instruction: 'I longed for Thy commandments' and 'My soul longed to desire Thy judgments.' The physical image of opening the mouth and drawing breath appears only here.
findings.after: Both verses use 'longed' for the speaker's yearning directed at God's instruction: 'I longed for Thy commandments' and 'My soul longed to desire Thy judgments.' The physical image of opening the mouth and drawing breath appears only here.

findings.finding: Jacob is not named in the shown Genesis 49:18 text.
findings.before: Both texts express waiting for the Lord's salvation: 'I awaited Thy salvation, Lord' and Jacob's 'I wait for the salvation of the Lord.'
findings.after: Both texts express waiting for the Lord's salvation: 'I awaited Thy salvation, Lord' and 'I wait for the salvation of the Lord.'

findings.finding: Only a general theme of deceitful speech; the wording differs ('deceitful tongue' vs 'deceitful lips and a boastful tongue'), and the source verse does not mention God or any response by Him, contrary to the rationale.
The source verse alone does not mention wicked speech, and the preceding verse it appeals to is not part of the shown source unit.
findings.before: Both texts use coals as a punishment for wicked speech. Psalms 139:10–11 says of those troubled by their lips that 'Coals will fall upon them', and the source names 'desert coals' in answer to the deceitful tongue of the preceding verse.
findings.after: Both texts name coals alongside an attack: the source joins 'desert coals' to 'The mighty one's sharpened arrows', and in Psalms 139:11 'Coals will fall upon them; in fire Thou wilt cast them down', said of those whom 'the trouble of their lips will cover'.

findings.finding: Nehemiah is not named in the shown verse (it says 'a man'), and the source's 'you' is not identified as God's people.
findings.before: Both texts speak of seeking good for God's people: 'I sought good things for you' and Nehemiah's arrival 'to seek good for the sons of Israel.' The source gives the motive as the house of the Lord our God.
findings.after: Both texts speak of seeking good: 'I sought good things for you' here, and in Nehemiah 2:10 Sanaballat and Tobia are displeased 'that a man had arrived to seek good for the sons of Israel.' The source gives the motive as 'the house of the Lord our God'.

findings.finding: The preceding clause naming the grandfather as Jesus is not part of the shown text, so that identification is drawn from outside the passages.
findings.before: The prologue says its subject, the translator's grandfather named in the preceding clause as Jesus, 'was himself moved to write something concerning instruction and wisdom'. Sirach 50:27 is the book's own notice that Jesus son of Sirach 'inscribed instruction' in this book and 'poured wisdom like rain from his heart', describing the same composition from the author's side.
findings.after: The prologue says its subject 'was himself moved to write something concerning instruction and wisdom', and Sirach 50:27 says that Jesus son of Sirach 'inscribed instruction in understanding and knowledge in this book' and 'poured wisdom like rain from his heart'.
