Both describe the writing of a book of instruction and wisdom; 50:27 names its writer.

findings.finding: Sirach 10:28 has no reward clause; 'give it honor according to its worth' is a second imperative, not a reward.
findings.before: Both verses open with the address 'Child' and an imperative to act 'with gentleness', followed by its reward: in 3:17 being loved by an acceptable person, in 10:28 the soul given glory and honor. The rewards differ, but the instruction to gentleness and its esteem is the same.
findings.after: Both verses open with the address 'Child' and an imperative to be carried out 'with gentleness': in 3:17 to carry out one's works with gentleness, with the promise of being loved by an acceptable person; in 10:28 to glorify one's soul with gentleness and give it honor according to its worth.

findings.finding: The claim that the phrase occurs only in these two places in the edition cannot be verified from the shown texts, and 'her' is not identified as wisdom in the shown verse.
findings.before: Wisdom's bonds are called 'a blue thread', the phrase used in Numbers for the 'blue thread' put upon the fringes of Israel's garments; in the edition the phrase occurs only in these two places. Numbers prescribes a garment law, while Sirach applies the thread figuratively to wisdom's bonds.
findings.after: The source says 'her bonds are a blue thread', the same phrase Numbers uses for the 'blue thread' put upon the fringes of the corners of Israel's garments. Numbers prescribes a garment law, while Sirach applies the thread figuratively to 'her bonds'.

findings.finding: Within the shown texts the link is only the word 'golden' in different ornaments (an ornament upon 'her' vs a collar around the neck). The rationale's claims that Proverbs ties the collar to instruction and that Sirach's 'her' is wisdom come from outside the shown verses.
Numbers 5:14 as shown states the case of a jealous husband; it does not give the procedure.
findings.before: Sirach warns, 'Do not be jealous of the wife at your bosom', while Numbers sets out the law for a man who 'is jealous of his wife'. Both address a husband's jealousy toward his own wife; Sirach advises against it, while Numbers gives the procedure when it arises.
findings.after: Sirach warns, 'Do not be jealous of the wife at your bosom', while Numbers sets out the case of a man who 'is jealous of his wife', whether or not she is defiled. Both address a husband's jealousy toward his own wife; Sirach advises against it, while Numbers legislates for when it arises.

findings.finding: 'Jerusalem and its allies' and suffering 'their rule' are not stated in the shown Jeremiah text.
findings.before: Sirach says 'do not teach her an evil lesson against yourself', and Jeremiah says 'you taught them lessons against yourself' and then suffer their rule. Both describe teaching others something that is turned against the teacher, though Jeremiah addresses Jerusalem and its allies rather than a husband and wife.
findings.after: Sirach says 'do not teach her an evil lesson against yourself', and Jeremiah says 'you taught them lessons against yourself for rule'. Both speak of teaching others something against oneself; Sirach applies it to a man and his wife, while Jeremiah addresses a 'you' whom labor pains will seize 'like a woman giving birth'.

findings.finding: 'Unfulfilled sight of good things' adds 'good things', which the shown source does not mention.
findings.before: Both Sirach passages use a eunuch's frustrated desire for a virgin as an image: here the eunuch embraces a virgin and groans, and in Sirach 20:4 the eunuch desires to take a young woman's virginity. The images illustrate different things, unfulfilled sight of good things here and judgment carried out by force there.
findings.after: Both Sirach passages use a eunuch's frustrated desire for a virgin as an image: here the eunuch embraces a virgin and groans, and in Sirach 20:4 the eunuch desires to take a young woman's virginity. The images illustrate different things: one who sees with his eyes and groans here, and the one who carries out judgments by force there.

findings.finding: No textual connection: no shared wording, image or person, only a thematic application of Sirach's general advice to the parable. The father in Luke divides property and does not give his son authority over him.
'Creation hymns' is not given in the shown texts, and Psalms 18:7 as shown does not name the sun.
findings.before: Both creation hymns describe the sun's overpowering heat: the psalm says no one will be hidden from his heat, and Sirach says the sun burns mountains three times as fiercely as a furnace. Only Sirach has the furnace comparison and the dimming of the eyes.
findings.after: Both describe overpowering heat from the heavens: Psalms 18:7 says of the one whose going out is from heaven's edge that 'there is no one who will be hidden from his heat', and Sirach says 'the sun burns mountains three times as fiercely' as a furnace. Only Sirach has the furnace comparison and the dimming of the eyes.

findings.finding: Sirach's verse does not name the moon, and Genesis 1:17 says 'them', not 'the lights'.
findings.before: Both place the heavenly light in the firmament of heaven to shine: Genesis 1:17 says God set the lights in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth, and Sirach describes the moon shining in the firmament of heaven. Only Sirach mentions the month taking its name from it and its changes.
findings.after: Both place heavenly bodies in the firmament of heaven to shine: Genesis 1:17 says 'God set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth', and Sirach describes the body from which 'the month takes its name' as 'shining in the firmament of heaven'. Only Sirach mentions the month and its changes.

findings.finding: Israel is not named in the shown Deuteronomy text; it says 'them'.
findings.before: Sirach calls the third people no nation, using the same expression as Deuteronomy 32:21, where God will provoke Israel with that which is no nation. Sirach applies it to a people he is disgusted with, while Deuteronomy uses it of the nation God will use to make Israel jealous.
findings.after: Sirach calls the third people 'no nation', the same expression as Deuteronomy 32:21, where God says 'I will make them jealous with that which is no nation'. Sirach applies it to a people his soul is disgusted with, while Deuteronomy uses it of what God will use to make jealous those who made Him jealous with that which is no god.

findings.finding: 'Solomon's carrying chair' and 'the Persian king's banquet hall' are not identified in the shown texts.
findings.before: Both describe royal furnishings built of silver and gold with pillars, purple and a stone pavement: Solomon's carrying chair here, and the Persian king's banquet hall with gold and silver couches on a stone pavement in Esther 1:6. Only the Song adds love from the daughters of Jerusalem.
findings.after: Both describe lavish furnishings of silver and gold with pillars, purple and a stone pavement: here pillars of silver, a gold reclining support, a purple step and an interior paved with stone; in Esther 1:6 purple cords upon gold and silver blocks, pillars of marble and stone, and gold and silver couches on a pavement of stone. Only the Song adds 'love from the daughters of Jerusalem'.

findings.finding: Wisdom 12:11 as shown does not say it concerns the former inhabitants of the land, and the source does not name 'the ungodly'.
findings.before: Both passages in Wisdom of Solomon call the ungodly an accursed offspring: here their offspring is accursed, and in 12:11 they were an accursed offspring from the beginning. Here the target is the ungodly generally, along with their wives and children, while 12:11 speaks of the former inhabitants of the land.
findings.after: Both passages in Wisdom of Solomon call a group an accursed offspring: here 'their offspring is accursed', alongside foolish wives and wicked children, and in 12:11 'they were an accursed offspring from the beginning', to whom God granted respite for their sins.

findings.finding: Neither shown text identifies its subject as the ungodly generally or the land's former inhabitants.
findings.before: Both passages in Wisdom pronounce the offspring of the wicked accursed: "an accursed offspring" here and "their offspring is accursed" there. The earlier verse speaks of the children of the ungodly generally, while this one concerns the land's former inhabitants, so it is an echo of the author's language, not an identification of a genealogical curse.
findings.after: Both passages in Wisdom pronounce an offspring accursed: 'an accursed offspring from the beginning' here and 'their offspring is accursed' in 3:12. Here it is said of those granted respite for their sins; in 3:12 it stands alongside foolish wives and wicked children.

findings.finding: Wisdom 12:25 as shown does not mention idolaters.
findings.before: Both verses describe God sending punishment upon idolaters matched to their lack of reason: "children without reason" receive judgment in mockery, and for "senseless reasonings" God sent "irrational animals." In both the address is "Thou didst send."
findings.after: Both verses describe God sending punishment matched to a lack of reason: 'children without reason' receive judgment in mockery, and in return for 'the senseless reasonings of their unrighteousness', by which they worshiped irrational creatures, God sent 'a multitude of irrational animals'. Both use the address 'Thou didst send.'

findings.finding: 'The same account of how idolatry arose' and the identification of the celebrants in 14:23 as idolaters are not in the shown texts.
findings.before: Within the same account of how idolatry arose, both verses link the cult to "mysteries" and "rites": the grieving father hands on "mysteries and rites," and idolaters celebrate "rites" and "secret mysteries." The later verse adds that the rites murder children, while here the rites honor a dead child.
findings.after: Both verses link cultic practice to 'mysteries' and 'rites': the grieving father who honored a dead human being as a god handed on 'mysteries and rites', and 14:23 speaks of 'celebrating rites that murder children, or secret mysteries'. The later verse's rites murder children, while here the rites honor a dead child.

findings.finding: In the psalm 'against God' belongs to speaking injustice, not to lifting the horn, and in Zechariah the horn is lifted against the Lord's land; the ellipsis merges the clauses.
findings.before: Both use the image of lifting a horn against God: the nations are "lifting a horn against the Lord's land," and the psalm warns "Do not raise a horn; do not lift your horn on high ... against God."
findings.after: Both use the image of lifting a horn in hostility: the nations are 'lifting a horn against the Lord's land', and the psalm warns 'Do not raise a horn; do not lift your horn on high', followed by 'do not speak injustice against God.'

findings.finding: That the angel 'first' speaks in 1:9 is not established by the shown texts.
findings.before: The figure here is "the angel speaking within me," the same interpreting angel who first speaks to Zechariah with "I will show you what these are."
findings.after: The figure here is 'the angel speaking within me', the same interpreting angel who says in Zechariah 1:9, 'I will show you what these are.'

findings.finding: The shown text of Zechariah 5:5 does not mention the measure, so calling it 'the measure vision' draws on outside context.
findings.before: The same "angel speaking within me" appears again in the measure vision, where he "came out" to direct the prophet; here he stands while another angel goes out to meet him.
findings.after: The same 'angel speaking within me' appears again in 5:5, where he 'came out' and directs the prophet to look; here he stands while another angel goes out to meet him.

findings.finding: The shown text of Zechariah 6:4 does not mention chariots.
findings.before: Zechariah asks "the angel speaking within me" the identical question, "What are these, lord?", in the vision of the chariots.
findings.after: Zechariah asks 'the angel speaking within me' the identical question, 'What are these, lord?', again in 6:4.

findings.finding: The 'vision of the horsemen' and the claim that the question 'first appears' there are not in the shown texts.
findings.before: The question "What are these, lord?" first appears in the vision of the horsemen, where the angel speaking within the prophet promises to show him.
findings.after: The question 'What are these, lord?' is also asked in 1:9, where 'the angel speaking within me' promises, 'I will show you what these are.'

findings.finding: In the source the speaker ('I') brings out the stone; the text does not say Zerubbabel brings it out.
findings.before: Both verses belong to the same oracle about Zerubbabel; the later verse says his hands laid the house's foundation and will complete it, which fits the stone he brings out here.
findings.after: Both verses concern Zerubbabel: here the great mountain is challenged 'before Zerubbabel' and the speaker will 'bring out the stone of inheritance', and in 4:9 'Zerubbabel's hands laid this house's foundation, and his hands will complete it.'

findings.finding: The source verse does not mention a lampstand.
findings.before: Revelation names "the two olive trees and the two lampstands," echoing this vision's pair of olive figures beside the golden lampstand; Zechariah speaks of olive branches and one lampstand.
findings.after: Revelation names 'the two olive trees and the two lampstands', echoing this vision's 'two olive branches'; Zechariah's verse speaks of olive branches beside golden nozzles and pouring channels rather than olive trees and lampstands.

findings.finding: The shown text of Zechariah 4:5 does not mention the lampstand.
findings.before: The same "angel speaking within me" questions the prophet in the lampstand vision, as here he invites him to look at what is coming out.
findings.after: The same 'angel speaking within me' questions the prophet in 4:5, 'Do you not know what these are?', as here he invites him to look at what is coming out.

findings.finding: The lead stone is thrown into her mouth; the text does not say she is shut in 'under a lead weight'.
findings.before: Both texts associate lawlessness with measuring tools: Micah asks whether "a lawless person" can be justified with deceptive weights, and here Lawlessness is shut in the measure under a lead weight.
findings.after: Both texts associate lawlessness with measuring tools: Micah asks whether 'a lawless person' can be justified with a balance and deceptive weights, and here Lawlessness is thrown into the measure and the lead stone into her mouth.

findings.finding: The only link is the bird name 'hoopoe' used in a simile; nothing else connects a winged-women vision with a dietary list, and the rationale's 'unclean birds' and 'food law' are not in the shown Leviticus verse.
That the angel was 'introduced in the first vision' is not established by the shown texts.
findings.before: The prophet again questions "the angel speaking within me," the same interpreting angel introduced in the first vision with "I will show you what these are."
findings.after: The prophet again questions 'the angel speaking within me', the same interpreting angel who says in 1:9, 'I will show you what these are.'

findings.finding: Nebuchadnezzar is not named in the shown Daniel text.
findings.before: Both texts place something in a house in Babylon: the measure is to have a house built for it there, and Nebuchadnezzar deposited the Lord's vessels in his idol-temple in Babylon.
findings.after: Both texts place something in a house in Babylon: a house is to be built for the measure 'in Babylon's land', and the Lord's sacred vessels were carried away to Babylon and deposited in an idol-temple.

findings.finding: Zechariah has the land mourning 'tribe by tribe', not 'family by family'.
findings.before: Matthew likewise says "all the tribes of the earth will mourn" when they see the Son of Man; Zechariah has the tribes of the land mourning family by family.
findings.after: Matthew says 'all the tribes of the earth will mourn' when they see the Son of Man; Zechariah has 'the land will mourn tribe by tribe'.
